questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unit vectors encode a direction in the plane
questions.stem: In the observatory notes, how do the two standard unit vectors describe a direction in the plane, and why is that description valid?

answer.exemplar: The unit vector along the x-axis and the unit vector along the y-axis point along the two coordinate axes and each has length one. Any direction with components (a, b) is written as a times the x-axis unit vector plus b times the y-axis unit vector, and the coefficients are exactly the projections of the direction onto the two axes, so the representation is unique once the axes are fixed.

questions.explanation: Unit vectors name a direction by its projections onto two fixed perpendicular axes. Because each has length one and the two are perpendicular, every coefficient is exactly the matching coordinate of the point.
questions.hint: Each unit vector has length one along its own axis.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Justify componentwise addition as a net displacement
questions.stem: In the log, why does adding two displacement vectors component by component agree with moving along one arrow and then the other?

answer.exemplar: Moving along the first arrow and then the second is the same trip as the straight-line displacement from start to finish, and that displacement has a horizontal part equal to the sum of the two horizontal parts and a vertical part equal to the sum of the two vertical parts. Because the two moves are independent in the x and y directions, the order of the legs can be swapped without changing the result, which is exactly what componentwise addition expresses.

questions.explanation: Chaining two arrows produces a net displacement whose horizontal and vertical parts are the sums of the corresponding parts of the two legs. The independence of the x and y directions is why the order of the legs can be swapped.
questions.hint: Compare the net trip with the component totals.

questions.stem: Why does a negative value of r in a polar entry still describe a point on the sky, and what does it change?

answer.exemplar: In polar coordinates the point sits on a ray at angle theta, at a distance given by the magnitude of r. questions.explanation: The radius is a signed distance along the ray, so a negative value sends the point the other way while keeping the same distance from the pole. Nothing is undefined; only the direction of the radius vector is flipped.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the area under a traced curve is not an integral against the parameter
questions.stem: In the log, why is the area under a traced curve not simply the integral of the y-coordinate against the parameter?

answer.exemplar: The area under a curve is a product of a height and a horizontal width, so the natural integral is the integral of y dx. When the curve is given parametrically, dx becomes x'(t) dt, and the factor x'(t) records how fast the curve is spreading horizontally at that moment. Integrating y against t alone measures a different quantity entirely, since it forgets the stretching of the horizontal direction.

questions.explanation: Area needs height times horizontal width, so the integral must be of y dx, and dx brings along the factor x'(t). The integral of y dt alone has no notion of horizontal width, so it does not measure area.
questions.hint: Area needs a height times a horizontal width.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a parameter adds to a pair of coordinate formulas
questions.stem: In the log, what information does the parameter carry that the equations for x and y do not?

answer.exemplar: The two coordinate formulas give the set of points on the curve, but the parameter also records the order in which they are visited, so a path that doubles back can be distinguished from one that does not. Two different parameters may also trace the same geometric curve while visiting it at different rates or in different directions, and only the parameter tells you which is which. The range of the parameter says which stretch of the curve is followed at all.

questions.explanation: The coordinate formulas fix the geometric set of points, while the parameter fixes the order and speed of the traversal. That extra information matters whenever a curve is retraced or a shape is drawn more than once.
questions.hint: The parameter records order and speed along the curve.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how unit vectors relate to coordinates
questions.stem: How do the two standard unit vectors relate to any vector written in coordinates?

answer.exemplar: Every vector in the plane can be written as a combination of the two standard unit vectors, which point along the positive x and y axes.
